analysis.one_liner: Bans new federal offshore oil, gas, and mineral drilling leases.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a House subcommittee and never received a vote, ending when the 112th Congress adjourned with 10 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act so that no new lease could be issued for oil, gas, or mineral exploration, development, or production in federal waters. Existing leases would not be affected; only new leasing would be shut off. It was introduced after the 2010 BP Deepwater Horizon spill, when coastal communities and members from spill-exposed states were pushing for a permanent drilling ban. The bill never advanced past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, fishing businesses, and tourism economies that bear the risk of offshore spills gain protection, since no new federal waters would be opened to drilling. Taxpayers avoid liability exposure from spills in newly leased areas. The general public gains from avoided spill risk, though with no new federal leasing, domestic offshore oil supply would not grow.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal communities and tourism and fishing economies

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits issuance of any new lease for exploration, development, or production of oil, gas, or any other mineral on the outer Continental Shelf [S2][S3].
Leaves existing leases untouched, so the ban applies only to opening new federal waters to drilling [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies lose access to future federal leasing, and the federal government forgoes potential royalty revenue from new production. Energy consumers could face somewhat higher prices or greater import reliance if domestic offshore supply does not expand.
analysis.who_pays_short: Offshore oil and gas companies and federal royalty revenue

drawbacks.text: Blocking all new outer Continental Shelf leasing would reduce future domestic offshore oil and gas production, which could put upward pressure on energy prices and increase reliance on imported oil [S2][S3].
The federal government and revenue-sharing coastal states would forgo royalty income that new leasing and production could have generated under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act [S3].
A blanket prohibition removes case-by-case decisions about which areas are appropriate for drilling, rather than setting environmental standards lease by lease [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a clear environmental protection — no new drilling in federal waters — at the cost of future domestic offshore production and the associated royalty revenue. For coastal communities whose livelihoods depend on unpolluted waters, the protection is direct; for the country as a whole, the tradeoff is lower potential energy supply against avoided spill risk. It was a blunt instrument, but a genuine one, and it never received any consideration on its merits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, which never acted, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced January 11, 2011 by Rep. Frank Pallone with Reps. Garamendi and Castor as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
Referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources, and on January 26, 2011 to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources [S5].
No further action was taken — no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate companion action appears in the record — and the bill expired at the end of the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013 [S5][S1].
The bill's cosponsors were all Democrats — 10 in total, alongside the Democratic sponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas producers are better off: no new-leasing ban was enacted, so future federal waters remained available to them. Members who opposed new drilling also avoided a recorded vote.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban new outer Continental Shelf leasing.

against.name: House Committee on Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out; the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee likewise took no action, keeping it from any vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 cosponsors and the sponsor were Democrats in a House whose majority was Republican; no Republican support appears in the record, and the Republican-run committee never took the bill up [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have shut off all future federal offshore leasing, eliminating these companies' access to new outer Continental Shelf acreage. Blocking new leasing keeps a spill-prone industrial activity out of federal waters that coastal residents and fishing and tourism businesses depend on.
A no-new-leasing rule reduces the risk of oil spills in federal waters that can close fisheries and beaches these businesses rely on. Their interest runs with coastal residents' interests.
